title: Supervised Learning Algorithms: KNN, SVM, Naive Bayes, LDA and QDA
description: How five classic supervised algorithms - KNN, SVM, Naive Bayes, LDA and QDA - turn labeled data into predictions, and where each one works best.
content:
**Supervised learning** trains a model on labeled data, where each training example is paired with an output label. The goal is to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs so the model can predict labels for new, unseen data. Supervised algorithms fall into two categories:
• Regression - the target is a continuous value (e.g., predicting a price)
• Classification - the target is a discrete class (e.g., spam vs. not spam)

**K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)** is used for classification and regression tasks. The prediction for a new data point is made from the majority class or the average value of its k nearest neighbours in the feature space.

How KNN works:
• It calculates the distance between the new data point and all other points in the training dataset.
• It selects the k nearest neighbours.
• Classification - the class is determined by the majority of those neighbours.
• Regression - the prediction is the average (or weighted average) of the neighbours' values.

Limitations of KNN:
• Computationally ineffective for large amounts of data.
• Performance deteriorates with high-dimensional or noisy data.

**Support Vector Machine (SVM)** is used for classification and regression tasks. Its primary objective is to find the optimal hyperplane that separates the data while maximizing the margin between the classes - maximizing the margin gives better generalization performance.

Key ideas behind SVM:
• Raw data is mapped into a high-dimensional space where it becomes linearly separable.
• A kernel is a mathematical function that transforms raw data into a high-dimensional space; kernels let SVM handle both linear and non-linear data.
• Common kernel functions: linear, polynomial, radial basis function (RBF), sigmoid.

**Naive Bayes (NB)** classifiers are probabilistic models based on Bayes' theorem. The "naive" part is the assumption that all features are conditionally independent given the class label.

Despite this strong and unrealistic assumption, Naive Bayes performs well in many practical applications - particularly on large datasets and high-dimensional data, such as text classification.

Types of Naive Bayes classifiers:
• Gaussian
• Multinomial
• Bernoulli

**Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)** is both a classification technique and a dimensionality reduction method. It makes two assumptions:
• Every class's data is distributed according to a multivariate normal.
• All classes share a common covariance matrix.

LDA provides a linear decision boundary, performs feature reduction and is computationally efficient - though its assumptions are not always valid on real data.

**Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)** is similar in spirit to LDA, but relaxes the equal-covariance assumption: each class is assumed to have its own covariance matrix. This flexibility allows QDA to capture more complex relationships between features and class labels by producing quadratic decision boundaries.

Quick comparison:
• KNN - instance-based, predicts from the k closest points; struggles with large, high-dimensional or noisy data.
• SVM - max-margin hyperplane; kernels extend it to non-linear problems.
• NB - Bayes' theorem with a conditional independence assumption; fast and strong on text and high-dimensional data.
• LDA - Gaussian classes with shared covariance, linear boundary, reduces dimensions.
• QDA - Gaussian classes with per-class covariance, quadratic boundary.
